title: Growing black holes may help create stars as well as shut star formation down
freshness: Published in The Astrophysical Journal and announced by the Center for Astrophysics on September 14, 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
excerpt: Astronomers studied nine nearby galaxies and found the same striking pattern around their actively feeding central black holes: rings of new stars alongside regions of disturbed gas. The result suggests black holes may sometimes help compress gas into new stars, rather than only heating or blowing star-forming material away.
whyItMatters: Black holes are usually pictured as destroyers that heat or blow away the gas needed to make stars. Finding the same pattern of star-forming rings, black-hole radiation and shocked gas across nine galaxies suggests their influence can be more complicated: in some places, the same activity that disrupts gas may also help compress it into new stars.

exploreFurther.label: Center for Astrophysics: New study reveals common pattern of black hole activity shaping nearby galaxies

body:
## The same pattern, nine times

Astronomers looked at nine nearby galaxies with actively feeding central black holes and found the same arrangement: rings of new stars, and, alongside them, regions of disturbed gas. The study was published in The Astrophysical Journal and announced by the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian on 14 September 2026. The DOI is 10.3847/1538-4357/ae9956. A German-language account at scinexx carries the same result.

Nine is not a huge sample. It is large enough that a repeated geometry is hard to dismiss as one galaxy’s quirk. The black holes are not quiet. They are accreting, which means gas is reaching the center and radiation and winds are coming back out. In the usual cartoon, that output heats gas or blows it away, and star formation shuts down. The cartoon is not wrong as a possibility. It is incomplete if the same galaxies also show new stars in rings.

## What was seen, and what is being inferred

Seen: rings of young stars, disturbed gas, and black-hole activity, together, in all nine systems. Inferred: the activity that stirs the gas can also compress some of it, and the compressed gas forms the stars in the ring. Compression is a physical step between “disturbed” and “a new star.” The observations show the endpoints — disturbed gas, young stars, an active nucleus — lined up in space. They do not show the gas parcel being squeezed and then lighting up. The inference is reasonable. It is still an inference.

Feedback is the name for this two-way influence. Energy leaves the vicinity of the black hole and changes the galaxy’s gas. Suppression is the famous direction. Triggered or assisted star formation is the other direction, discussed for decades and harder to catch cleanly, because young stars have other reasons to form in rings. A bar in the galaxy, or a resonance in the disk, can pile gas into a ring without any help from the black hole. The paper’s case is that the black-hole radiation and the shocked gas sit in the same pattern as the rings, across nine galaxies, which would be a coincidence if the nucleus were irrelevant. “Would be a coincidence” is the structure of the argument. Read the ApJ paper for how they tried to rule the coincidence out.

## Why the destroyer picture sticks, and why it should loosen

Black holes are easy to narrate as destroyers because the energy numbers are so one-sided. A small fraction of the rest mass of accreted gas, released as light and kinetic power, rivals the output of the galaxy’s stars. That power can empty a halo. It can also hit a cloud and shove it into collapse if the geometry is a shell or a ring rather than a direct hit. Both outcomes can be true in different places in the same galaxy, at the same time. The nine-galaxy pattern is evidence that the second outcome is common enough to show up as a repeated structure, not a one-off.

Nothing here says black holes are net producers of stars, or that they built these galaxies. It says the local effect is mixed: suppression in some gas, star formation in the ring. A net budget would need masses and rates this note does not take from the press release.

The CfA announcement is the clearest secondary account. The ApJ article is the authority for the measurements. scinexx is an additional report, not an independent dataset. The useful next idea is feedback as a map, not a switch: where the energy goes, and which gas it hits, decides whether the next generation of stars is smaller or gets a push.
